## EXERCISE 1: LINEAR REGRESSION
In this exercise we will work on a slightly modified version of a dataset on birth weights (reported in Dunn & Smyth 2007). I would also like you to share a companion paper on this by one of my favourite statisticians, none other than Dr Andrew Gelman. You will find the paper here:
https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/unpublished/standardizing.pdf Links to an external site.

In the data-file, BirthWeight_dat.csv Download BirthWeight_dat.csv, you will find four columns of data, BirthWeight: bodyweight at birth [lbs]; GestationalAge: gestational age at birth [weeks], BW_mat: maternal bodyweight [kg], T1DM: maternal type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosis (1: yes, 0: no).

A. Examine the data through data tables and visualisations.

B. Develop a simple linear regression, interpret and discuss the model coefficients. How would you explain these effects?
C. During the lecture series I talked about testing interaction effects on the most important main effects. Well, let's try this here.
Refine the above regression model by adding an interaction effect between GestationalAge and T1DM.
Reinterpret the coefficients. In words, describe the effect of the interaction. How does your interpretation of the main effects (that are included in the interaction) differ now?

D. A remedy to the above interpretation challenge is to centre the independent variables that are included in the interaction term.
Do this and reinterpret the output.

E. Why would you want to standardise independent variables? Try this out and reinterpret the output.
F. Under what situations would you want to log-transform the dependent variable? Independent variables? How would this affect your interpretation of the coefficients?

```{r}
## import the data
birth_dat <- read.csv("BirthWeight_dat.csv")

# A: examine data for example using summary(data), plots, pairs, etc.
summary(birth_dat)
pairs(birth_dat)
hist(birth_dat$BirthWeight, xlab = "Birth Weight [lbs]")
# note: the DV is approximately normal and continuous data

# B: carry out a regression analysis
# with the following model:
m1_t1 <- lm(BirthWeight ~ GestationalAge + BW_mat + T1DM, data = birth_dat)
summary(m1_t1)
plot(m1_t1)

# INTERPRETING COEFFICIENTS:
# Intercept: -2.58
# Birth weight at a gestational age of zero, maternal body weight of zero
# and mother without type 1 diabetes mellitus.

# Gestational Age - Beta=0.16
# Is the change in birth weight if gestational age increases with one week,
# keeping all other inputs constant. 

# BW, mother - Beta=0.10
# The change in birth weight if maternal BW differs by one KG, keeping all other
# inputs constant.

# T1DM - Beta=1.47
# Change in birth weight if mother suffers from T1DM, keeping all other
# inputs constant.

# C: interaction effect
# then, with the following model:
m2_t1 <- lm(BirthWeight ~ GestationalAge*T1DM + BW_mat, data = birth_dat)
summary(m2_t1)
plot(m2_t1)

# Interaction GestationalAge:T1DM, Beta=0.05
# The effect of gestational age is increased by 0.05 if the mother suffers from
# T1DM.
# The main effects should now be interpreted as setting the other main effect in the 
#  interaction to zero. 

# D: CENTERING DATA
# CENTERING: 
# helps us to interpret main effects in the presence of interaction effects
# We now can interpret the main effect as its effect when the other main effect is 
# the average.

# We simply center by deducting the mean from the data, so that:
AgeCentred <- birth_dat$GestationalAge - mean(birth_dat$GestationalAge)

birth_dat2 <- data.frame(birth_dat, AgeCentred)

m3_t1 <- lm(BirthWeight ~ AgeCentred*T1DM + BW_mat, data = birth_dat2)
summary(m3_t1)
plot(m3_t1)

# We could also center by any other reference value of our choice

# E: STANDARDISATION
# can be used to better help us compare Beta coefficients.
# comparison of beta coefficients are subject to differences in scales between
# predictors. 
# One workaround is to standardise the independent variables, for example:
# Age_std <- (Age - mean(Age))/(sd(Age))
# Age_std <- (Age - mean(Age))(2*sd(Age))

# We can now interpret all coefficients on roughly the same scale.
# A benefit of scaling by 2*sd is that 1-unit change in the predictor leads to
# a change from 1 sd below the mean to 1 sd above the mean. This maintains coherence
# when we are working with binary effectors. 
# The intercept is now the average DV with all IVs at their mean.

GestationalAge_std <- (birth_dat$GestationalAge -
                         mean(birth_dat$GestationalAge))/(2*sd(birth_dat$GestationalAge))
BWmat_std <- (birth_dat$BW_mat - mean(birth_dat$BW_mat))/(2*sd(birth_dat$BW_mat))

birth_dat3 <- data.frame(BirthWeight = birth_dat$BirthWeight, GestationalAge = GestationalAge_std,
                         BW_mat = BWmat_std, T1DM = birth_dat$T1DM)

m4_t1 <- lm(BirthWeight ~ GestationalAge*T1DM + BW_mat, data = birth_dat3)
summary(m4_t1)
plot(m4_t1)

# Another alternative (in models without interactions), is to leave IVs as they are
# and then rescale the beta coefficients by multiplying with 2*SDs. 
# This will allow a rough comparison of coefficients. 

# F: NONLINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS
# NONLINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS IN CASE OF VIOLATING THE ASSUMPTION OF ADDITIVITY AND LINEARITY:
# LOG-TRANSFORMATION OF Y: %-change in Y per 1-unit increase of X.
# LOG-TRANSFORMATION OF X: Change in Y per % change in X.
# LOG-Y, and LOGX: % change in Y per % change in X

# Ref: Gelman 2007: https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/unpublished/standardizing.pdf

```

## EXERCISE 2A: SURVIVAL IN LEUKAEMIA - SURVIVAL ANALYSIS
Import the data-file, Leukaemia_dat.csv Download Leukaemia_dat.csv. The data-file contains four columns: Time: Surival time [days]; WBC: white blood cell count, AG: genetic type (1 or 2), Status: 1: deceased. 

Take a look at the data and propose an analysis.
Develop a simple model and have a go at interpreting the model parameters. 

```{r}
# import data
leuk_dat <- read.csv("Leukaemia_dat.csv")

summary(leuk_dat)
pairs(leuk_dat)
hist(leuk_dat$Time, xlab = "Survival Time [days]")

# note: suggest survival analysis as DV is time-to-event

# carry out survival analysis
library(survival)

# first we create a survival object
leuk_obj <- Surv(time = leuk_dat$Time, event = leuk_dat$Status)

# perform Kaplan-Meier estimation
leuk_km <- survfit(leuk_obj ~ 1)
summary(leuk_km)

# plot the Kaplan-Meier curve
plot(leuk_km, xlab = "Time [days]", ylab = "Survival probability",
     main = "Kaplan-Meier curve")

# interpretation of KM plot: 
# a rough estimate of the cumulative probability of surviving a given time over time.

# fit a cox proportional hazards regression model
m1_cox <- coxph(leuk_obj  ~ leuk_dat$WBC + leuk_dat$AG)

# then test the proportional hazards assumption (ok in this case)
cox.zph(m1_cox)

# look the outputs:
summary(m1_cox)

# Interpreting the cox proportional hazards model output:
# coef: are the Beta-coefficients of the model.
# se(coef): the standard errors of the coefficeints.
# z: is the z-score (n standard errors Beta is away from zero).
# Pr.. : probabvility of Beta estimate being zero. 
# exp(coef): these are the hazard ratios of the model parameters.
# exp(-coef): the inverse hazard ratios.

library(survminer)
ggforest(m1_cox, leuk_dat)

# Hazard ratios: the relative chance of an event. E.g., HR = 3, it is three times
# as likely that the event occurs given the treatment parameter (in this case AG).

```

## EXERCISE 2B: COUNT DATA & POISSON REGRESSION
Import the data-file, LungCancer_dat.csv Download LungCancer_dat.csv. This is data on the number of lung cancer metastases across patients. 
The data-file contains three columns: MetCount: numbers of metastases (count); Gene: presence of a genetic biomarker; Biomarker: levels of an antigen.

Propose a modelling method and develop a simple model.
Interpret and present the model coefficients. 

```{r}

## Importing the data
lc_dat <- read.csv("LungCancer_dat.csv")
summary(lc_dat)
pairs(lc_dat)
hist(lc_dat$MetCount)

# note: the DV is count, and has a typical exponential distribution.
# Hence, Poisson regression is suitable.

# fit a Poisson GLM 
m1_2b <- glm(MetCount ~ Gene + Biomarker, family = poisson(link = log), data = lc_dat)

# DHARMa can be used to produce diagnostic plots of most GLMs
# The DHARMa vignette:
# https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DHARMa/vignettes/DHARMa.html
library(DHARMa)

sim_res <- simulateResiduals(m1_2b)
plot(sim_res)

# plot the distribution of the residuals: these look ok
library(sm)
m1_res <- residuals(m1_2b, type = "deviance")
sm::sm.density(m1_res, model = "normal")

# Let's look at the summary output for the model:
summary(m1_2b)

# Interpreting the model output:
# Poisson regression uses a log-link. So that:
# log(MetCount ~ B0 + B1*Gene + B2*Biomarker)
# comment: deviance of model is significantly better compared to the null model.
# And, Deviance is smaller than the degrees of freedom suggestion that overdispersion
# is not an issue. We now look at the estimates of the coefficents.
# We should interpret coefficients following exponential transformation. So, in this case:

# Intercept: -2.73, this is the Log(MetCount) when the remaining IVs are Zero.
# Or the count, exp(-2.73)=0.07, or close to zero.

# Biomarker Beta = 0.75, or exp(0.75)=2.12. 
# This is a multiplicative factor on the normal scale.
# Which means that Metastasis Count increases by 112% per increase of one in Biomarker.

# Gene Beta = 0.50, or exp(0.50)=1.65.
# So, with the same logic, Metastasis Count will increase by 65% due to gene expression.

# Incidence Rate Ratio:
# This can be calculated as exp(Beta) and represents the Ration in count due to one
# unit difference in the independent variable. 

## Plotting data:
#  could be useful both on log and normal scale to better understand the impact of 
#  a given variable.
Gene_spec <- 1
Gene <- rep(Gene_spec,100)
Biomarker <- seq(from = 2.5, to = 7.5, , length.out = 100)

data_new <- data.frame(Gene, Biomarker)

pois_pred <- predict(m1_2b, data_new)

obs_dat1 <- filter(lc_dat, Gene == Gene_spec)

plot(obs_dat1$Biomarker, obs_dat1$MetCount, xlab = "Biomarker", ylab ="MetCount")
lines(data_new$Biomarker, exp(pois_pred))

plot(obs_dat1$Biomarker, log(obs_dat1$MetCount), xlab = "Biomarker", ylab ="Log(MetCount)")
lines(data_new$Biomarker, pois_pred)

# model param 95% confidence intervals:
m12b_ci <- confint(m1_2b)
exp(m12b_ci)

```

## EXERCISE 2C: BINARY OUTCOMES & LOGISTIC REGRESSION
Import the data-file, TitanicSurvival_dat.csv Download TitanicSurvival_dat.csv. This is data of the recorded survivals and deaths on the Titanic.
The data-file contains four columns, Survived: 1: yes, 0: no; Sex: female or male; Age: age in years; Class: the passenger class (1st, 2nd and 3rd class).

Propose a modelling method and develop a simple model. 
Interpret and present the model coefficients.

```{r}

# importing the data
titanic_dat <- read.csv("TitanicSurvival_dat.csv")

summary(titanic_dat)
hist(titanic_dat$Survived, xlab = "Survived (=1, else =0)")

# note: the DV is of a binary outcome, hence suggesting binomial logistic regression

# We perform logistic regression on Survival
m1_2c <- glm(Survived ~ Sex + Age + Class, family = "binomial", data = titanic_dat)
summary(m1_2c)

library(DHARMa)
sim_res <- simulateResiduals(m1_2c)
plot(sim_res) # ok

### Interpreting the output:
## Overview:
# The coefficients are the log(odds). Meaning that the exp(coef.) is the odds ratio of survival
# in this case. So, for every unit increase in an IV (holding other constant)
# the log(odds) will increase/reduce multiplicativelty by the log(odds).

# All coefficients are negative, in this case meaning that 
# male, Age and lower passenger classes (2 and 3) are associated with lower odds of survival.

# Sex, male: -2.50
# For categorical variables we can look at the exponents of hte coefficient to get
# the odds. In this case, exp(-2.50) = 0.08
# Meaning, males had 0.08 times the survival odds of females.

# Class, 2nd: -1.28
# Again, exp(-1.28)=0.27. 2nd class had 0.27 times the survival odds of 
# first class passengers.

# Class, 3rd: -2.30 -> exp(-2.3)=0.10
# 3rd class passangers had 0.10 times the survival odds as first class passengers.

# Age: -0.03, exp(-0.03)=0.97
# A difference in age of 1 corresponds to a negative difference of -0.03 in the logit
# probability of survival.

## Some alternative interpretations:
# Interpretation 1:
# We can evaluate the model at two Ages of interest and look at the difference in
# probability. For example a Child of 10 and an adult of 40 years of age.

delta_prob <- (1/(1+exp(3.522 - 0.034*10))) - (1/(1+exp(3.522 - 0.034*40)))
# The difference in probability is 0.06, or 6% (when keeping all else at zero)

# Interpretation 2:
# Dividing Beta by 4 gives us an upperbound of the difference in probability.
# In this case we get: -0.034/4 = -0.0085. A difference in age by one year corresponds
# to no more than a 0.85% difference in probability in survival.

# Interpretation 3:
# Odds ratio. So, exp(-0.034)=0.97
# So, a difference in Age of one, corresponds to a multiplicative change in the odds
# by 0.97. For example changing the odds from 1 to 1*0.97=0.97.

# Alternative 4: predicting and plotting the probability curves
# For example, if we want to simulate probability of survival for a given group

Sex_spec <- "male"
Class_spec <- "3rd"

Sex <- c(rep(Sex_spec, 100))
Class <- c(rep(Class_spec, 100))
Age <- seq(from = 1, to = 80, length.out = 100)

data_pred <- data.frame(Sex, Age, Class)

# Predict
pred <- predict(m1_2c, data_pred, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)

# Convert to probabilities
data_pred$fit <- plogis(pred$fit)

# obs data plot
library(dplyr)
titanic_dat2 <- filter(titanic_dat, Sex == Sex_spec & Class == Class_spec)

# plot
plot(titanic_dat2$Age, titanic_dat2$Survived, xlab = "Age [Yrs]", ylab = "Prob. Survival", title = "Sex: male, Class: 2nd")
lines(data_pred$Age, data_pred$fit, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Odds ratios
m12c_or <- exp(coef(m1_2c))
# Confidence intervals
exp(confint(m1_2c))

# ROC curve (We will talk more about this in Lecture 5B)
# ability of model to discriminate between outcomes
# Sensitivity: true positive / (true positives + false negatives) -> correctly identifying that someone Survived. 
# Specificity: true negatives / (true negatives + false positives) -> correctly identifying the deceased. 
# Used to determine prediction threshold, e.g.:

library(pROC)
m1_pred <- predict(m1_2c, type = "response")
titanic_dat3 <- na.omit(titanic_dat)
m1_roc <- roc(titanic_dat3$Survived, m1_pred)
plot(m1_roc)
auc(m1_roc)

# assessment
coords(m1_roc, x = 0.5, input = "threshold", ret = c("sensitivity", "specificity"))
# sensitivity: 0.70, specificity: 0.84

# prediction, e.g.: Balance between sens. and spec.
coords(m1_roc, "best", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"))

# threshold: 0.37, sens: 0.79, spec: 0.76

```

## EXERCISE 2D: ORDINAL OUTCOMES & ORDINAL REGRESSION
The dataset in mood_dat.csv (Mood_dat.csv Download Mood_dat.csv) contains the measure of mood in three levels (DV: 1 = anxious, 2 = indifferent, 3 = relaxed) following a pain stress test (X1 = 1, or no pain stress test, X1 = 0), and as a function of Age [years].
Import the data-file, TitanicSurvival_dat.csv. This is data of the recorded survivals and deaths on the Titanic.

Propose a modelling method and develop a simple model. 
Interpret and present the model coefficients.

```{r}

## Import the mood data
mood_dat <- read.csv("Mood_dat.csv")

summary(mood_dat)
pairs(mood_dat)

# note: the DV is of an ordinal categorical scale. 

# Carry out ordinal logistic regression using polr() in MASS
library(MASS)

mood_dat$DV <- as.factor(mood_dat$DV)

m1_2d <- polr(DV ~ Age + X1, mood_dat)
summary(m1_2d)

# As for logistic regression, we can work with Odds ratios by exponentiation of the
# coefficients.
# We assume that the effect is constant for the three categories. This is the 
# proportional odds assumption.

# So, in this case we have the effect of Age:
# Proportional odds exp(-0.068)=0.93. So the multiplicative effect of increase
# in age by one year is 0.93. Mood reduces with age.

# X1: pain stress test
# exp(-1.588)=0.20. The multiplicative effect of doing the pain stress test
# is 0.20. Or, individuals who performed the pain stress test had 0.20 times the
# odds of individuals who did not perform the pain stress test.
# the intercepts are the logg odds of the boundaries on a continuous scale.
# a log odds less than one is a probability lower than 0.5.


### Plotting probabilities across variables
Age <- seq(from = 18, to = 80, length.out = 100)
X1 <- rep(1, 100)

data_new <- data.frame(Age, X1)

m1_predprobs <- predict(m1_2d, data_new, type = "probs")

# plot model probabilities for the three levels
ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(data_new$Age,m1_predprobs[,1],colour = "anxious")) +
  geom_line(aes(data_new$Age,m1_predprobs[,2],colour = "indiff")) +
  geom_line(aes(data_new$Age,m1_predprobs[,3],colour = "relaxed")) +
  xlab("Age [years]") +
  ylab("Response")


```
